newsitem.title: JAPAN: Scandal penalties would hit Japan's Yamaichi hard.
newsitem.headline: Scandal penalties would hit Japan's Yamaichi hard.

text.p: Unlike mighty Nomura Securities, which is expected to weather stiff penalties for its role in a racketeer scandal, its weaker rival Yamaichi could take a body blow if it suffers the same fate, industry analysts say.

Prosecutors on Thursday raided the homes of Yamaichi Securities Co Ltd's top executives, in search of evidence of suspected illegal deals with a racketeer at the heart of a huge scandal that already ensnared Nomura Securities Co Ltd and Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank Ltd (DKB), one of Japan's biggest banks.
The move followed a raid on Yamaichi offices on Wednesday by Tokyo prosecutors and a government watchdog, the Securities Surveillance and Exchange Commission.
Prosecutors have said they suspected that Yamaichi paid 79 million yen ($669,000) to corporate extortionist Ryuichi Koike, already charged with accepting payoffs from Nomura and DKB.
Such payoffs have been banned since 1983.

A government source said on Wednesday that Yamaichi had generally admitted the illegal transactions and Japanese media said on Thursday that the brokerage's top officials, president Atsuo Miki and chairman Tsugio Yukihara, would soon resign over the affair.
The emergence of the scandal just as Tokyo kicks off its "Big Bang" financial reforms, aimed at boosting competition, has made authorities keen to take a stern stance against lawbreakers.
At the same time, "Big Bang" deregulation is expected to result in a big industry shake-up and the failure of smaller brokerages, as commission revenue drops and competition grows.

The Finance Ministry on Wednesday unveiled harsh penalties against DKB and Nomura, including a ban until year-end on Nomura's proprietary stock trading and on participation in the auction and underwriting of public bonds.

Nomura's profits, by far the strongest among domestic brokers, are sure to suffer in the current business year to March 1998. But many analysts expect them to woo back clients and remain a top player in Japan's increasingly open markets.
Prospects for Yamaichi would not be as rosy should the firm be hit with similar penalties, the analysts said.

"Yamaichi doesn't have the equity cushion that Nomura has...and in terms of business mix it is not as well-positioned to respond to deregulation," said Robert Garone, an analyst at Dresdner Kleinwort Benson Securities.

"Even without the scandal, Yamaichi would have had a very difficult time securing its position in the changing environment. The scandal makes it that much harder and increases the probability of the company having serious problems," he added.

Investors appeared to agree with this assessment of the two brokerages' differing outlooks. On Thursday, Nomura shares rose 100 yen to 1,680, while Yamaichi's fell 20 yen to close at 260. They were the two most-heavily traded issues on the first section of the Tokyo bourse.

Yamaichi suffered a 5.43 billion yen ($46.0 million) parent current loss in the April-June quarter after posting a 1.22 billion yen ($10.3 million) current profit in 1996/97. It posted a parent net loss of 164.76 billion yen ($1.39 billion) in 1996/97 because of steps taken to help a non-bank financial subsidiary dispose of problem loans.

Credit rating firm Japan Bond Research Institute (JBRI) said on Wednesday it would review its rating for bonds issued by Yamaichi for possible downgrading due to the scandal. "The potential is that the influence of administrative punishment will be relatively large compared to other firms in the same industry," JBRI said in a statement.
Some analysts said harsh penalties might force Yamaichi to seek support from other financial institutions. Others said the situation might not be so dire, at least in the short term.

"Yamaichi's balance sheet...looks weak compared to some other firms, so proportionately the impact would be far greater," said one foreign analyst. "But to talk about the company's collapse is quite premature."

Many experts who had thought the scandal would end after authorities made object lessons of Nomura and DKB expressed surprise that a relatively weak firm was now in the spotlight, In the end, though, the tough official policy could be beneficial for Japan's markets and its financial industry.

"If anybody commits illegal action, they will pay for it no matter what. If you're going to have a capital market which people view with credibility, that's the way the rules have got to be set," Garone said. ($1=118 yen)
